name: Sign Editor Open
desc: Opens the sign editor GUI for a specific sign position.

writeup.p: One field, one purpose: the BlockPos of a sign the player may edit. The server sends it when the player right-clicks an edit-eligible sign (EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign), and the client opens GuiEditSign over that position. It is the request half of the sign edit flow; the committed text returns as C12PacketUpdateSign. It is the only play-state packet that forces a GUI open purely from coordinates, which makes it the canonical trigger point for sign automation.

handleSignEditorOpen dispatches on the main thread, reads the tile entity at the position, and if it is not a TileEntitySign it fabricates one, attaches the world and position, then calls thePlayer.openEditSign. Because the handler constructs the tile entity, the packet works even when the sign block is not client-loaded, a quirk automation could lean on. Server side the producer is EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign, which sends S36 built from the sign's position.

Zero module hits across all 8 clients. The mined grep returns only the vanilla handler, the EntityPlayerMP producer, the EnumConnectionState registration and the packet class, plus Rise 6.x script API registration. Auto-sign modules that auto-fill shop or claim signs would hook exactly this packet and answer with C12PacketUpdateSign, but none exists in Memeware, Nekoware, Rise, Sigma, Spicy or Tenacity. The metadata draft for an AutoSign module has no corpus backing and is omitted.

The packet is clientbound and only changes GUI state, so there is no exploit surface worth the name. A server can spam it to force the editor open, which is an annoyance rather than an exploit; the client honors it only while in game. Nothing validates, rate-limits or acknowledges it, and no anti-cheat measures it. The practical module use is benign: observing when the server grants edit rights, then answering with a pre-filled C12.

implementation.overview: The sign edit prompt: one BlockPos that makes the client open GuiEditSign. It is the request half of the sign flow, with the text committed separately via C12PacketUpdateSign. No module in the 8-client corpus hooks it, so the impl is a vanilla-only story about a GUI state transition with no exploit surface.
implementation.server_handling: EntityPlayerMP.openEditSign sends it with no validation beyond the right-click interaction; the server never tracks whether the client opened the editor. The sign text is only committed when C12PacketUpdateSign arrives, so S36 is a prompt rather than a lock: the server cannot tell an auto-filled response from a typed one.
implementation.protocol_notes: A single BlockPos encoded as the 1.8.9 packed long. PLAY state only. The packet implies a stateful client transition (GUI open) but carries no transaction id, so duplicates or reordered packets simply reopen the editor. This is also why modules cannot correlate a specific S36 with a specific C12 without tracking the position themselves.
implementation.anticheat_landscape: Irrelevant to anti-cheats: no movement, timing or combat signal. Servers that police auto sign filling do it by pattern-matching C12PacketUpdateSign text and measuring the latency between open and commit against human behavior. No module in the corpus exists to trigger such heuristics anyway.
implementation.general_hooks: The natural hook surface is PacketReceiveEvent, but no module in the 8-client corpus registers one for S36; Rise 6.x only adds the class to its script NetworkAPI whitelist.
implementation.client_variations: All 8 clients carry the byte-identical vanilla handler; the only non-vanilla reference anywhere in the corpus is the Rise 6.x script API registration.

anticheat.overview: The sign editor open packet has an empty corpus: the sweep for S36PacketSignEditorOpen and PacketPlayOutSignEditorOpen returns zero hits across all 50 anticheats. The packet only flips GUI state, so anticheats police sign interaction on the commit side instead. NCP's AutoSign times the gap between the server granting edit rights and the C12PacketUpdateSign commit, and Intave's ItemCrashTracker.checkSign validates the returned sign lines; the open prompt itself carries no abuse signal and nothing in the corpus reads it.
